title: Hyundai Glovis Partners with Shopee to Serve 700 Million E-Commerce Users - Retail News Asia

 Why it matters
 Hyundai Glovis has launched end-to-end logistics with Shopee Korea, consolidating domestic pickup, customs, freight, and fulfillment for beauty brands into a single contract. 
 The deal challenges fragmented forwarders and regional integrators by serving Shopee's 700 million users across Southeast Asia, Taiwan, and Brazil with predictable shipping timelines. 
 Watch for operational expansion from core Southeast Asian hubs into Brazil, alongside progress towards Glovis generating 40 percent non-affiliated revenue by 2030. 
 Retail News Asia newsroom analysis
 Hyundai Glovis began operating an end-to-end logistics partnership with Shopee Korea this month, taking over the complete supply chain for domestic cosmetics brands expanding abroad.
 The agreement links the freight forwarder to Shopee’s customer base of about 700 million users across Southeast Asia, Taiwan and Brazil, packaging international shipping into a single contract.
 Announced on Monday, the collaboration handles cross-border operations as Hyundai Glovis targets raising non-affiliated business to 40 percent of its total revenue by 2030.
 Consolidating the Cross-Border Chain
 Under the arrangement, merchants receive a single service point covering domestic cargo pickup in South Korea, air and ocean line-haul, export-import customs clearance, in-country regulatory filings and destination fulfillment. Previously, cosmetics labels contracted separate logistics handlers for domestic trucking, international freight and destination deliveries. That fragmentation created handoff delays and customs clearance bottlenecks at regional entry ports.
 Cross-border cosmetics exporters regularly encounter divergent health authority approvals across Southeast Asian jurisdictions, where labeling regulations and ingredient clearances vary between markets. Handling domestic regulatory compliance directly allows merchants to avoid third-party agency handoffs that routinely slow inventory onboarding.
 Diversifying Beyond Captive Car Hauling
 For Hyundai Glovis, handling consumer parcel flow serves a long-term commercial balance sheet target. The company wants non-affiliated commercial contracts to generate 40 per cent of its total corporate revenue by 2030.
 Carriers serving South Korean e-commerce have historically struggled with unit economics on low-weight parcel shipments compared to bulk automotive and industrial cargo. Running cross-border beauty logistics shifts Glovis into higher-frequency retail operations, competing against dedicated regional integrators and postal networks. Success depends on whether consolidated freight pricing beats the decentralized local forwarders merchants currently use.
 Export Demand Drives Freight Integration
 South Korean cosmetics manufacturers have leaned harder into direct platform exports as consumer appetite for premium skincare formulas climbed across Southeast Asia and Latin America. Rather than building local retail store footprints or signing sole distributorships, mid-tier beauty labels increasingly use marketplace storefronts to test market appetite before committing physical capital.
 Shopee operates dominant marketplace market shares across Southeast Asia, alongside expanding operations in Brazil. Supplying those territories with consolidated freight infrastructure gives platform sellers predictable delivery timelines against local beauty retail alternatives.
 Next Steps for Latin America
 Initial rollouts focus on South Korean sellers fulfilling consumer orders into Southeast Asian markets. The companies plan to extend the service footprint into Brazil and other Latin American territories once operations across the primary Asian hubs stabilize.
 Execution hinges on Glovis meeting delivery timetables while building non-captive freight volume toward that 2030 target.

 Consolidating fragmented shipping will likely succeed for Hyundai Glovis because direct export beauty brands require smooth regulatory and customs clearance across disparate Southeast Asian markets. The tie-up immediately pressures decentralised local forwarders and postal networks, which historically relied on disconnected handoffs. However, the commercial risk lies in parcel unit economics; shifting from bulk automotive cargo to lightweight retail consignments strains margins if consolidated pricing fails to undercut entrenched competitors. Glovis must maintain strict delivery timetables across Asian hubs before unlocking volume in Latin America. Watch the rollout date for the planned Brazilian expansion.
 Maria Santos
 Questions & Answers
 Q. What logistics services are consolidated under this new partnership?
 A. The arrangement provides South Korean cosmetics exporters with a single service point covering domestic cargo pickup, air and ocean line-haul, customs clearance, destination fulfilment, and in-country regulatory filings. This eliminates the need for merchants to contract separate logistics providers for each stage.
 Q. Why is Hyundai Glovis expanding into cross-border e-commerce fulfilment?
 A. The contract helps the company diversify away from captive car hauling and bulk industrial cargo towards higher-frequency retail operations. Hyundai Glovis aims to generate 40 per cent of its total corporate revenue from non-affiliated commercial contracts by 2030.
 Q. How does the partnership address regulatory challenges for cosmetics brands?
 A. Southeast Asian markets enforce differing ingredient clearances and labelling regulations. By handling domestic regulatory compliance and filings directly under a single contract, the service removes the third-party agency handoffs that typically cause customs bottlenecks and delay inventory onboarding.
 Q. When will the logistics service expand to Latin America?
 A. The initial rollout focuses on South Korean sellers shipping to Southeast Asian markets. The companies plan to expand the service into Brazil and other Latin American territories once operations across the primary Asian hubs have stabilised.
